title: Decision: Diageo Scotland Limited v The Coal Authority
text:
LANDS TRIBUNAL FOR SCOTLAND

Citation: [2025] LTS 7 , Case reference: LTS/COMP/2023/0002

OPINION OF THE TRIBUNAL

Tribunal members: RA Smith KC , Mr A Oswald FRICS , Mrs D Lovell

Diageo Scotland Limited
Applicant
against
The Coal Authority
Respondent

Subjects: Bonnybridge Bonded Warehouses, 151 Glasgow Road, Dennyloanhead, Bonnybridge
Application for determination of a question of disputed compensation

Applicant: Burnet KC , Advocate; Addleshaw Goddard  LLP
Respondent: Lindsay KC , Advocate; DLA Piper UK  LLP

17 April 2025

Introduction

[1] This is an application under section 40 of the Coal Mining Subsidence Act 1991 (“the 1991 Act”) to deal with certain disputes as to whether the respondent is obliged to take remedial action in terms of section 2 of that Act. The applicant (“Diageo”) own bonded warehouses at their site in Bonnybridge used for the maturation of whisky. The respondent (“the Authority”) is successor to the British Coal Corporation under the 1991 Act. Settlement at two warehouses and a sinkhole (also described as a crown hole) have appeared at Diageo’s site. A damage notice under section 3 of the 1991 Act was served upon the Authority on or about 12 May 2020.

[2] The Authority contends that damage had occurred more than 6 years prior to service of the notice, ie prior to 13 May 2014, and accordingly Diageo’s application is time‑barred. By the time of the hearing, the Authority accepted that the claim in respect of the sinkhole was not time-barred, but maintained its position regarding the settlement damage. Diageo accept that settlement damage had occurred by 2008 at the latest. However it contends that despite undertaking reasonable inquiries it was not in a position prior to 13 May 2014, to conclude that the damage was likely to be “subsidence damage”. “Subsidence damage” is defined in section 1 as damage caused by the withdrawal of support from land in connection with coal mining operations. In the event that a notice triggering a requirement for the Authority to take remedial action is time‑barred, Diageo contends that there was fresh damage in 2017 and thereafter, for which the notice is not time‑barred.

[3] The Authority does not accept that the settlement and sinkhole are related to coal mining operations. However, parties have agreed, for the purposes of a preliminary hearing on time‑bar, that the causal mechanism of the settlement at Warehouse No. 1 occurring by or about 2008 is the same mechanism for the settlement as occurred in 2017. The position of Diageo is that the mechanism at least partly involved the withdrawal of support from land in connection with mining operations.

Procedure

[4] We held an accompanied site visit on 18 March 2025. We held a hearing on 19 March on the preliminary question of time‑bar. Diageo produced five witnesses who gave evidence by affidavit. Their evidence was not challenged. The witnesses were Mr Karl Rennie who was formally a contracts manager at Marshall Construction Limited and had been involved in works at the site for many years, since around 1992/1993. Mr Peter Kerridge is a civil and structural engineer at Blyth & Blyth Consulting Engineers Limited (“Blyth & Blyth”). He has been with that firm since 2007 and was first involved at the site in about March 2015. Mr Phillip Ham is managing director of Envireau Limited (“Envireau”) since 2017 and had worked with that business since 2007. He has a Masters degree in Civil and Environmental Engineering and also a PhD in Environmental Hydrology. His involvement with the Bonnybridge site began in 2020.

[5] The applicant also led the evidence of Mr Matthew Jackson who is a business leader, has been with Diageo for 28 years and worked as site manager at Bonnybridge between 2015 and 2020. We also received the evidence of Anne Boyle. She is a past employee of Diageo and is now a contractor. She was involved in investigating and recovering documents concerning the dispute. Parties also produced a joint minute agreeing the tenor of the documents in this case, including reports.

[6] The applicant was represented by Mr Alasdair Burnet KC and the respondent was represented by Mr Mark Lindsay KC .

Statute

[7] The Coal Mining Subsidence Act 1991 provides:

“ 1.— Subsidence damage to which Act applies.

(1) In this Act ‘subsidence damage’ means any damage—

(a) to land; or

(b) to any buildings, structures or works on, in or over land,

caused by the withdrawal of support from land in connection with lawful coal-mining operations.

(2) An alteration of the level or gradient of any land not otherwise damaged which does not affect its fitness for use for the purposes for which, immediately before the alteration occurred, it was used, or might reasonably have been expected to be used, shall not be regarded as damage for the purposes of subsection (1) above.

…

2.— Duty to take remedial action.

(1) Subject to and in accordance with the provisions of this Part, it shall be the duty of the British Coal Corporation (‘the Corporation’) to take in respect of subsidence damage to any property remedial action of one or more of the kinds mentioned in subsection (2) below.

(2) The kinds of remedial action referred to in subsection (1) above are—

(a) the execution of remedial works in accordance with section 7 below;

(b) the making of payments in accordance with section 8 or 9 below in respect of the cost of remedial works executed by some other person; and

(c) the making of a payment in accordance with section 10 or 11 below in respect of the depreciation in the value of the damaged property.

…

3.— Notice of subsidence damage.

(1) The Corporation shall not be required under section 2(1) or (4) above to take any remedial action or make any payment in respect of the cost of emergency works, unless the owner of the property or some other person who is liable to make good the damage in whole or in part—

(a) has given to the Corporation the required notice with respect to the damage within the period allowed by this section; and

(b) has afforded the Corporation reasonable facilities to inspect the property, so far as he was in a position to do so.

(2) The required notice with respect to any subsidence damage is a notice stating that the damage has occurred and containing such particulars as may be prescribed; and references in this Act, in relation to any subsidence damage, to a damage notice are references to such a notice with respect to the damage given within the period allowed by this section.

(3) The period allowed by this section for giving a damage notice with respect to any subsidence damage is the period of six years beginning with the first date on which any person entitled to give the notice had the knowledge required for founding a claim in respect of the damage.

(4) For the purposes of subsection (3) above, the knowledge required for founding a claim in respect of any subsidence damage is knowledge—

(a) that the damage has occurred; and

(b) that the nature of the damage and the circumstances are such as to indicate that the damage may be subsidence damage;

and a person's knowledge includes knowledge which he might reasonably have been expected to acquire from the facts mentioned in subsection (5) below.

(5) Those facts are—

(a) any facts which were observable or ascertainable by him; and

(b) any facts which would have been ascertainable by him with the help of any expert advice which it was reasonable for him to seek.

…

40.— Disputes: general.

…

(2) Where in any proceedings under this Act the question arises whether any damage to property is subsidence damage, and it is shown that the nature of the damage and the circumstances are such as to indicate that the damage may be subsidence damage, the onus shall be on the Corporation to show that the damage is not subsidence damage.

…”

Cases

Darley Main Colliery v Mitchell (1886) 11 App Cas 127
West Leigh Colliery Company Limited v Tunnicliffe & Hampson Limited (1907) H.LE.
Duke of Abercorn v Merry & Cunninghame (1909) SC 750
Dunlop v McGowans 1980 SC (HL) 73
Severn Trent Water Ltd v Coal Authority [2005] RVR 21
ANW Group Ltd v Gilcomston North Ltd 2008 SLT 835
Pelagic Freezing (Scotland) Limited v Lovie Construction Limited [2010] CSOH 145
Wood v Coal Authority [2010] UKUT 193 (LC)
Newbold v Coal Authority [2016] UKUT 432 (LC)
Sciortino v Beaumont [2021] Ch 365.
Noble v Barr [2022] PNLR 19
Tilbury Douglas Construction Ltd v Ove Arup & Partners Scotland Ltd 2024 SC 383

Textbook

Gordon, Scottish Land Law (3 rd ed) 5-113

Background facts and circumstances

[8] Diageo operate nine bonded warehouses at the site. Warehouse Nos. 1 to 6 were constructed in the 1970s, and numbers 7 to 9 were constructed in 2008. Warehouses 1 and 2 are to the north of the site, with Warehouse 1 being to the west of No. 2. Warehouse 6 is to the south and west of Warehouse 1. The warehouses are very large and are divided into sections or cells.

Settlement damage

[9] Mr Rennie speaks of wall cracking and floor sinking in Warehouse No.1 in the 1990’s. An area of Warehouse 1 was modified from storage to form a disgorging trough whereby a section of sunken floor was re-laid with new concrete to suit the new levels for the trough. He recalls carrying out various pointing and temporary mortar repairs to the cracking. He recalls cracking in the division cell walls of Warehouse 6 and carrying out further repairs. He recalls this work being carried out in about 2005.

[10] Blyth & Blyth were instructed to carry out monitoring works on the two warehouses over a period from May until August 2008, with subsequent monitoring in March 2009. Their report of 24 March 2009 describes defects in Warehouse Nos. 1 and 6 as floor dipping, the line of racking varying from horizontal and extensive cracking in the division walls. Mr Kerridge specifically mentions a dip in the aisle flooring of Warehouse No. 1. Their report states that survey results demonstrated that there appeared to be no ongoing settlement at that time but further monitoring of the warehouse floors was recommended.

[11] A detailed site investigation was instructed and works were undertaken by the Mason Evans Partnership Limited (“Mason Evans”). Mason Evans provided reports dated January and December 2009. A detailed desktop investigation was carried out, and soil and mineral boreholes were undertaken along with geotechnical testing and groundwater monitoring. The subsequent report had the benefit of further investigation although its terms are generally similar to the former report.

[12] Mason Evans found that there are no less than nine coal seams in the vicinity of the site, as recorded in the Bonnyrigg No. 2 mineshaft lying to the north of the site. They found historical evidence of mine working under part of the site. There was also a nearby gravel pit where sand and gravel extraction had been carried out.

[13] Of relevance to the present case the December 2009 report contained the following:

“Geotechnical assessments

…

Made ground

7.2.1 Investigations recorded thick made ground deposits across the majority of the site, comprising variable proportions of silt, clay, sand and gravel with various extraneous fragments including colliery waste. The made ground was conjectured to be associated with in filling of former sand and gravel quarries …

Conclusions

7.6.1 The recorded ground conditions and geotechnical assessment indicated thick deposits of poorly consolidated made ground do exist beneath much of the site, particularly beneath the western portion of Bonded Warehouse No. 1 and beneath the majority of Bonded Warehouse No. 6 …

7.6.3 In consideration of the existing foundations, which appear to be placed on the poorly consolidated main ground soils and weak/variable natural soils (external columns and foundation bearing slab), the likelihood that settlement within the warehouses has been caused by settlement of the variable and generally poor quality superficial soils, was considered likely.

Mining conditions

8.3.5 The No.4 Dennyloanhead hard coal (0.50m to 1.30m thick) was encountered beneath the site at shallow depths, outcropping through the central site area. Evidence of mine workings was indicated by the presence of packed wastes (and possible mine roof collapse up to 2.70m thick) and the loss of air flush during the drilling operations, which was consistent with the available mine plan information. Therefore, we have concluded that the Dennyloanhead hard coal has been worked at shallow depths beneath the entire northern site area.

General principles of surface instability

8.4.1 Deterioration within old mine workings can lead to collapse a considerable time after abandonment. The mechanisms of failure are varied and complex but generally involve either a yield in the roof of the mine between supports, or collapse as a direct result or failure of the supports.

8.4.2 Except in instances where the mine workings are very shallow for example, less that 10m deep, the stability is comparatively unaffected by loadings from buildings or by vibrations from heavy traffic. Progressive deterioration within the workings can, however, advance to a stage where instability is reached and collapses occur. In most cases, however, it is impossible to predict with any degree of accuracy if, and when, such movements will take place.

8.4.3 Accordingly it is generally accepted that old abandoned mine workings are susceptible to collapse. Researches based on observations and past experience do, however, permit some assessment of the likelihood of any collapses within the mines being experienced at the surface as subsidence. It is also possible to make reasonable assessments of the magnitude of movements which may occur under assumed failure conditions.

8.4.4 The subsidence assessments consider various elements of the geological and mining configuration. These include the nature and thickness of the rock and soil overburden, the extracted height of the workings and typical mine configuration.

8.4.5 In our assessments we have sought to achieve a rock/overburden cover thickness of 10 times the seam extraction height for a stoop and room mining extraction. This is consistent with a number of recent studies in the field of mining stability assessment.

Surface instability due to mining

8.5.1 Our researches and investigations have confirmed that mine workings exist at the level of the Dennyloanhead hard coal at shallow depths beneath the central and northern site areas. As the seam was recorded to be generally 1.0m thick, at least 13.00m of rock overburden would be required above the workings to preclude at the surface instability constraints.

8.5.2 As there is less than 13.00m solid rock cover above the seam over the central and northern site areas (beneath Bond Nos. 1 and 6), these areas can be considered to be minerally unstable. Therefore, surface instability as a result of shallow mine workings in the Dennyloanhead hard coal could be a contributing factor to the surface instability experienced within Bonded Warehouse Nos 1 and 6, and could also lead to future subsidence of the buildings …

Surface instability constraints and remedial recommendations

General

9.1.1 Based on the existing documentary information, subsidence recorded within Bonded Warehouse Nos. 1 and 6 was most likely caused by the following:

(1) Differential settlement due to foundations being constructed on poor soils

(2) Surface instability due to collapse of shallow mine workings.

9.1.2 Investigations have therefore been undertaken to assess the ground conditions in the vicinity of these warehouses and to discount/prove either of the potential instability sources.

Differential settlement associated with poor soil conditions

…

9.2.3 In consideration of the existing foundations, which appear to be placed on the poorly consolidated made ground soils and weak/variable natural soils, the primary cause of settlement within the warehouses was conjectured to have been caused by stress and settlement within the superficial soils …

Mineral instability associated with shallow mine workings

9.3.1 The investigations and researches recorded shallow mine workings within the Dennyloanhead hard coal to exist within critical depths of the surface. Consequently surface instability associated with mine collapse beneath the site cannot be discounted.

9.3.2 While the primary cause of instability was considered to be differential settlement within the made ground/natural soils, the likelihood that mine collapse could result in surface instability sometime in the future cannot be ruled out. Therefore it is recommended that a mine consolidation programme is undertaken as part of the remediation works. We would revert you back to us in this regard at the appropriate time.

…”

[14] There was no mine consolidation programme carried undertaken following upon the 2009 reports.

[15] Blyth & Blyth provided an update report of September 2015, in respect of Warehouses Nos. 1 and 6, and it was confirmed that no further settlement had been recorded in the floor in the period from August 2009 to August 2015. In an addendum report of 23 October 2015 it was confirmed that rack alignment deformation which was out of tolerance in Warehouse 1 did not pose any risk of instability or collapse in their current condition. In Warehouse 6 there were no racks out of tolerance. It was recommended that if further surveys indicated that the floor was continuing to settle and the racks were moving further out with the relevant tolerance, that further review be undertaken on the stability of the racking system and precautions introduced as required to stabilise the structure.

[16] A noticeable increase in cracking at Warehouse No. 1 occurred in 2017. Mr Rennie refers to cracks going horizontally and up the whole side of the wall, brick and blockwork snapping in half, blocks falling loose and debris coming away from the wall. He refers to a noticeable difference with the earlier damage with the cracks being larger, more of the block work had come loose and there was more debris lying on the floor. One of the warehouse cells was no longer used after this point.

[17] Mr Jackson refers to receiving a call in July 2017 while on holiday, and being told of a substantial change in the cracks on the internal walls of Warehouse No. 1 and debris on the floor. He refers to the damage being so bad he could physically take out parts of the wall by hand.

[18] Blyth & Blyth attended on 7 July and in their report of December 2017 referred to extensive cracks being witnessed with crack widths between 10‑15mm. A large amount of block fragments and debris was witnessed on the floor due to the cracking and spoiling of blockwork walls. A load bearing structure began to impose loading on the racking structure causing the balustrade adjacent to a compartment wall to buckle along its length. Pre-cast concrete column enclosures appeared loose or to have demonstrated signs of movement, and were described as potentially unsafe. Floor slab settlement occurred as much as 15mm. In a report of November 2018 Blyth & Blyth recommended the amount of loading on the racking in cell 1B to be reduced similar to that carried out in cell 2B. Annual checks were recommended.

[19] So to conclude there was significant settlement affecting Warehouse No. 1 by 2008 at the latest, in which the damage comprised cracking of walls, settlement of floor slabs and misalignment of internal racking. An affected area was repurposed with racking being removed. Warehouse No. 6 also suffered some damage. Between 2009 and 2015 it can be concluded that there was no further settlement at Warehouse 1. However in 2017 further settlement damage occurred, being noticeably worse than the 2008 settlement damage, occurring in approximately the same area. This further and substantially affected Diageo’s operations at the western part of the warehouse.

The sinkhole / crown hole

[20] On or about April 2016 a hole appeared in the ground close to the northern aspect of Warehouse 2. Diageo arranged for the hole to be filled in by Marshall Construction Limited, which work was carried out on or about 16 June 2016. The area had been the site of earlier flooding. Blyth & Blyth had attended in March 2015. They provided a solution to control the water and channel it into the drainage system. No conclusion was reached as to where the water was coming from, although it was found not to be a burst pipe as previously thought possible.

[21] On 23 February 2020 a hole of several metres in diameter appeared at the same location as the previous hole.

[22] The damage notice having been served on or about 12 May 2020, the Authority undertook a site inspection in May 2020. In September the Authority backfilled the hole with approximately 48 tonnes of clean stone, being approximately the equivalent to a volume of 30m³.

Diageo’s submission

[23] The onus of proof was upon the respondent to establish time‑bar. It was submitted firstly that the applicants despite undertaking reasonable enquiries were not in a position prior to 13 May 2014 to conclude that the pre‑2009 damage was likely to be “subsidence damage” as defined. Diageo’s second argument was that even if requisite knowledge existed for the pre‑2009 damage, there was a fresh cause of action for the 2017 damage which was not time‑barred.

[24] Turning to the first argument, more specifically, there required to be knowledge, in terms of section 3(4)(b):

“that the nature of the damage and circumstances are such as to indicate that the damage may be subsidence damage; and a person’s knowledge includes knowledge which he might reasonably have been expected to acquire from the facts mentioned in subsection (5) below.”

Those facts included those “which would have been ascertainable by him with the help of any expert advice which it was reasonable for him to seek”.

[25] In this respect it was accepted that the Mason Evans reports of January and December 2009 were in play. However it was submitted that these did not provide a basis to serve a damage notice on the Authority. Reference was made to the executive summary of the December 2009 report stating:

“In consideration of the exiting foundations, which appear to be placed on the poorly consolidated made ground soils and weak/variable natural soils, the primary cause of settlement within the warehouses was conjectured to have been caused by settlement of the variable superficial soils.”

It was emphasised that the word “conjectured” had been used and that the “primary” cause did not relate to coal mining. Emphasis was also given to the words that: “the likelihood that mine collapse could result in surface instability sometime in the future cannot be discounted” did not necessarily provide the trigger for a damage notice. To serve a damage notice in 2009 would have be in contradiction to the advice of the experts stating that the primary cause was the fact the foundations were based upon made ground. Diageo’s position was that in retrospect the pre 2009 damage may have been more likely to have been caused by mine workings.

[26] Turning to the second argument, counsel emphasised that section 1 of the 1991 Act focused upon “damage”. It was accepted that the pre‑2009 damage was not de minimis in the sense of subsection (2). However the 2017 damage could be seen as “new” subsidence damage, there having been at least 6 years of no settlement between 2009 and 2015. This conclusion was supported by the evidence of monitoring. The witness evidence indicated that the 2017 settlement damage was substantially worse.

[27] It was submitted that for the purposes of section 3, the cracking observed in 2008 and the damage occurring in 2017 were separate instances of “subsidence damage” occurring at different times, albeit at the same location. It was agreed that the same mechanism caused the subsequent cracking, but that was not the same as saying that the 2017 damage was the same as the 2008 damage. If it was too late to claim in relation to pre‑2009 damage it did not mean that it was too late to claim in respect of the 2017 damage.

[28] The authorities addressed the time at which a claim for subsidence damage due to the withdrawal of underground support, on account of underground mine workings, starts to run. This is when the damage occurs to property on the surface. Subsequent claims can be made in respect of further damage to the same property.

[29] Reference was made to Darley Main Colliery Company v Mitchell which found that it was the damage, and not the excavation, which resulted in the cause of action. A cause of action in respect of further subsidence damage to the same property was a new cause of action and did not arise until that particular subsidence damage occurred: Lord Halsbury at p. 133, Lord Bramwell at p. 147. This view was adopted in Scotland in Duke of Abercorn v Merry & Cuninghame , Lord Mclaren at p. 753.

[30] Reference was also made to West Leigh Colliery Company v Tunnicliffe & Hampson Limited indicating that damages were due for the extent of damage actually occurred to property at the surface. No account was taken of the potential diminution in value of the subjects due to the possibility of further damage. Consistently, it was clear that there was no prohibition on making subsequent claims in relation to later damage to the same area of land. Reference was also made to Gordon, Scottish Land Law at 5 – 113.

[31] In response it was submitted that the cases cited by the Authority were not in point. The cases did not relate to claims for subsidence damage, where different common law rules applied.

[32] An example of the correct approach was Newbold v Coal Authority. The issue related to whether coal mining caused a second phase of subsidence damage after the 1980’s. The Upper Tribunal found that evidence of recent large scale movement did not establish that changes as had occurred since a certain date, were as a result of mining subsidence. In other words, had such recent changes been as a result of mining subsidence, there would have been a valid claim.

[33] Counsel concluded that the authorities permitted two separate causes of action, namely for subsidence damage and further subsidence damage respectively. The causes could be seen as being different in either temporal or locational terms. There was no doubt, for example, that the sinkhole was in close proximity to the settlement damage to Warehouse No.1 and it was not suggested that a claim in respect of the sinkhole had the same cause of action as the claim in respect of pre‑2009 damage. It was a question of degree. The purpose of the Act would not be fulfilled if there was a small amount of damage in year one, but then severe damage 20 years later at the same location, if a claim to remedy the latter damage was time‑barred.

Coal Authority’s submission

[34] The claim in respect of Warehouse No. 1 was time‑barred. There was only one cause of action and this accrued in 2008 – 2009 at the latest. The further damage in 2017 was not a new or separate cause of action and it was irrelevant that the 2017 damage was more serious.

[35] In terms of the 1991 Act the Authority had no duty to take remedial action under section 2 until a damage notice had been served under section 3. That notice would be time‑barred if issued more than 6 years after the time when an applicant had the requisite knowledge in terms of section 3(4) and in particular subparagraph (b) and subsection (5). It was accepted that damage had occurred by 2009, but Diageo did not argue that the damage was de minimis .

[36] It was accepted that the common law should fill in the blanks in interpreting the statute. The statute did not deal with the issue here, namely whether subsequent damage in effect gave rise to a second claim which would not, therefore, be time‑barred in the event that a claim for earlier damage had become time‑barred. It was accepted that section 18 provided for dealing with both original damage and further damage, but this only applied where there had already been a valid damage notice for the original damage. The Act did not deal with the situation we have here, where the damage notice was invalid in respect of the original damage.

[37] It was submitted that the single action rule was trite law and the authorities did not permit “salami slicing” a claim in order to avoid prescription. Counsel referred to numerous cases, mainly from the sphere of negligence and professional negligence. Reference was made to Sciortino v Beaumont, Noble v Barr, Dunlop v McGowans, ANW Group Limited v Gilcomston North Limited, Pelagic Freezing (Scotland) Limited v Lovie Construction Limited and Tilbury Douglas Construction Limited v Ove Arup & Partners Limited. In Noble v Barr The Irish Court of Appeal at [44] concisely summarised English law as follows:

“It is a long established rule at common law that if a plaintiff has suffered actionable damage as a result of a defendant’s breach of duty, in a case where damage is the gist of the action (such as negligence), he can and must claim damages in a single action for all the damage which he has suffered or will suffer in consequence of that breach of duty … Once any actionable damage is suffered, time begins to run. Any further damage that may subsequently arise from the same breach of duty does not give rise to a further cause of action. All damage, including prospective or contingent damage must be claimed in the first action; the ‘rule is that damages for loss resulting from a single cause of action will include compensation not only for damage accruing between the time that the cause of action arose and the time that the action was commenced, but also for the future of prospective damage reasonably anticipated as the result of the defendant’s wrong, whether such future damage is certain or contingent.’”

[38] Counsel provided a detailed analysis of the authorities which demonstrated that the common law in Scotland and England was materially the same, and resulted in the same conclusion namely that there was only one cause of action which accrued in 2008/2009, and the damage in 2017 did not give rise to a new and separate cause of action.

[39] Turning to the authorities relied upon by Diageo, it was submitted that properly understood, Darley Main did not support the proposition that each incidence of subsidence damage gave rise to a new cause of action. It was limited to its circumstances where a claim for earlier damage had been compensated in full, and later damage had been caused by a failure to take the necessary remedial action to prevent further subsistence occurring in the future. It was that latter failure which gave rise to the new cause of action. Counsel founded upon the speeches of Lord Fitzgerald at p. 151 and Lord Bramwell at p. 146, who along with Lord Halsbury were in the majority.

[40] Lord Bramwell and Lord Fitzgerald founded on the fact that the mechanism for the subsequent damage, at the same location, was different to the mechanism for the first damage. That was not the case here, since parties agreed that the mechanism of the second damage was the same as the first.

[41] It was also submitted that West Leigh Colliery was of limited assistance because the issue was not time‑bar, but an issue whether a claim could lie for depreciation in the value of the surface owner’s property. It was held an action did not arise where the supposed loss was brought about merely by market depreciation concerning future risk of damage to the property. Limited weight could be given to Duke of Abercorn which related to a right to claim for further subsidence on a distinct area of ground to the area of ground which had been subject to an earlier claim.

[42] Turning to the issue of Diageo’s knowledge in 2009, it was pointed out that no witness had spoken to how Diageo reacted to the Mason Evans reports. There was no explanation why, for example, the recommendation to undertake a mine consolidation programme as part of the remediation works, was not followed through.

[43] Counsel emphasised section 3(4)(b) on the matter of knowledge, which states “that the nature of the damage and the circumstances are such to indicate that the damage may be subsidence damage …” Reference was also made to section 40(2) which also used the word “may” in the context that the damage and circumstances were such to indicate that the damage may be subsidence damage, the onus would be on the Authority to show that the damage was not subsidence damage.

[44] It followed that the knowledge threshold for serving a damage notice was not high and a limited amount of evidence was required to engage the section. Reference was made for example to Wood v Coal Authority at [76].

[45] There was also a shifting evidential burden in section 3. The Lands Tribunal in Severn Trent Water v Coal Authority said:

“17. In our judgment section 3 of the 1991 Act, as it falls to be applied in the present case, imposes the legal burden on the claimant but provides for a shifting evidential burden of proof. It is for the compensating authority to establish matters which, they say, would constitute facts for the purposes of section 3(5) and from which they assert that the claimant could reasonably have acquired the knowledge required for founding a claim. If they do so the burden is then on the claimant to show, in relation to such matters, that it could not reasonably have been expected to acquire the requisite knowledge from them.”

Reference was also made to Newbold v Coal Authority at [326] and [327].

[46] Here the Mason Evans reports stated that surface instability associated with mine collapse beneath the site “cannot be discounted”. In other words the reports were saying that mine collapse was possible; ie the damage “may” be subsidence damage. Looking at the reports in context, they were referring to both current (ie 2009) and future surface instability. The reports made a positive recommendation for a mine consolidation programme. In these circumstances the onus was back on the applicant to show it could not reasonably have had the knowledge required for founding a claim.

[47] Absent an explanation why the recommendation was not followed, it had to be concluded that Diageo had had the requisite degree of knowledge to found a claim, standing the low threshold required for a damage notice. The 2017 damage to Warehouse No.1 was accordingly time‑barred.

Discussion

Time‑bar – knowledge

[48] The 1991 Act provides in section 2 a duty upon the Authority to take remedial action in respect of subsidence damage to any property. In terms of section 1(1) “subsidence damage” means damage to land or buildings etc “caused by the withdrawal of support from land in connection with lawful coal mining operations.” The duty in section 2 is triggered in section 3(1) by the giving of a damage notice by the owner of the property. Section 3(3) further provides that the period allowed for giving a damage notice is 6 years beginning with the first date on which any person entitled to give the notice had the knowledge “required for founding a claim in respect of the damage.”

[49] Critical to the present case is subsection 4(b) providing that the knowledge required for founding a claim is knowledge:

“… that the nature of the damage and circumstances are such as to indicate that the damage may be subsidence damage; and a person’s knowledge includes knowledge which he might reasonably have been expected to acquire from the facts mentioned in subsection (5) below.”

Subsection (5) provides for any facts which would have been ascertainable by the property owner with the help of any expert advice which it was reasonable to seek.

[50] As has been pointed out, the expression that “the damage may be subsidence damage” in subsection 4(b) ties in with the onus of proof set out in section 40. All that an applicant requires to do in terms of section 40 is show that the damage “may” be subsidence damage, and the onus then falls upon the Authority to show that the damage is not subsidence damage. In other words, once an applicant is armed with good evidence of the knowledge referred to in section 3(3), and serves the damage notice, the onus falls to the Authority to show that the damage is not subsidence damage, ie not damage caused by withdrawal of support from land in connection with lawful coal mining operations.

[51] These provisions are part of what is essentially a compensation scheme, and are no doubt intended to address the difficulty which a property owner would otherwise face, of proving that the possible subsidence damage is indeed, on balance of probability, subsidence damage. In this respect we note, for example, that the prescribed notice is relatively straightforward and does not require detail as to the mechanism of the subsidence.

[52] The question here is whether with the assistance of its experts, Diageo had knowledge in 2009 that the pre‑2009 damage may be subsidence damage. We accept the applicant’s argument that the word “may” in section 3(4) indicates a relatively low threshold for the knowledge required for founding a claim.

[53] It is apparent that the Mason Evans work carried out on behalf of Diageo in 2009 was extensive. The reports go into considerable detail and found upon many sources of information, including historical mining and mapping records, as well as their own ground investigations. We need not go into extensive detail here. The problem encountered was undoubtedly complex, as there were two potential scenarios, namely settlement from made ground, probably the result of the infilling of a sand and gravel quarry, and subsidence of shallow coal mining operations further below. The report is perhaps inevitably cautious, using words such as “conjecture” in respect of the made ground scenario (paragraph 9.2.3 of December 2009 report). Nevertheless the report still says that the “primary cause” was likely to be settlement within the made ground (paragraph 7.6.3). This part of the report would of course have pointed against any claim against the Authority.

[54] However reading the report as a whole, Mason Evans were concluding that mine collapse was a real possibility. The insufficient rock overburden to preclude surface instability is explained in some detail. In paragraph 8.5.2, for example, the report states that the shallow mine workings “could be a contributing factor” to the instability experienced within Warehouse Nos. 1 and 6, and could “also” lead to future subsidence. It is in these circumstances that Mason Evans state that mine collapse could “not be discounted.” We find it difficult to interpret the report in any way other than knowledge is imparted that the damage “may“ be subsidence damage within the meaning of section 3, at least in the sense that it may be a contributory factor to the damage.

[55] In reaching this conclusion we have some sympathy for Diageo, in that the “primary” cause was said to be something else, and in terms of its position only with hindsight did mining related subsidence appear more likely. But the fact that the report also recommended mine consolidation measures is an equally strong indicator that the past mining operations posed risks of continuing damage. We do not know why this part of the report was not followed up. If there was a subsequent informed view that the mining operations were sufficiently remote not to be a significant factor in the damage, and justified inaction, it was not imparted in the evidence.

[56] Accordingly we would uphold the Authority’s argument on this point. The damage occurring up to 2008/2009 is time‑barred because more than 6 years elapsed before service of the damage notice on 12 May 2020.

Single or separate cause of action

[57] We now turn to the question of whether a claim in respect of the 2017 damage is precluded because a claim for the pre‑2009 damage is, as we have found, time‑barred. This must depend upon whether the 1991 Act requires a claim in respect of subsidence damage to be treated as a once and for all claim.

[58] The Act contains fairly detailed provisions about remedial action once the Authority has accepted a claim. There is provision for whether the Authority, or the applicant, carries out the remedial work with the applicant being reimbursed in the latter case. The Authority may make payment in lieu of remediation work. Where it appears probable that further subsidence damage will occur within a period of 18 months from the date of the damage notice, the Authority may issue a stop notice in respect of remediation work.

[59] The foregoing provisions were not discussed in detail but passing reference was made to section 18. This provides that where there is a damage notice, and further subsidence damage has become evident, the original damage and further damage shall be treated as one and, where the Authority have elected to make a payment in lieu of executing remedial works, a fresh damage notice is required.

[60] We mention this because it appears that the Act recognises inherent difficulties with subsidence damage, which are also apparent from the expert evidence in this case. Subsidence damage is unpredictable. It may or may not progress over time. It may progress slowly. Or it may appear or reappear suddenly. It may reach a “natural” extent, or it may not.

[61] It seems to us that their Lordships in dealing with the 19 th / early 20 th century loss of support cases were aware of these sort of peculiar difficulties. For example, in Darley Main Lord Fitzgerald says at p. 150:

“This appeal represents a class of cases peculiar and exceptional, to meet which and to avoid grave convenience, if not injustice, how flexible common law has somewhat moulded itself.”

[62] It is also the case that the right to compel the Authority to take remedial action in the 1991 Act is not dissimilar to the common law under discussion in the mining subsidence cases. In each, the question is whether surface damage has occurred by withdrawal of support from land in connection with coal mining operations. Therefore, we are not attracted to the approach in modern negligence actions where the single action rule applies, where the rule has not been developed in the context of land law. The single action rule, as it existed at the time, yielded in the common law mining cases. We would think, in any event, that if it is appropriate to draw analogy with negligence cases, the type of continuing loss of support which may be occurring in this case is more consistent with the concept of continuing wrongdoing. In this scenario, there is separate provision in the relevant statute to escape the effect of the single action rule.

[63] Turning to Darley Main, Diageo rely upon the following passage of Lord Halsbury at p. 133:

“But the words ‘cause of action’ are somewhat ambiguously used in reasoning upon this subject; what the plaintiff has a right to complain of in a court of law in this case is the damage to his land, and by the damage I mean the damage which in fact had occurred, and if this is all that a plaintiff can complain of, I do not see why he may not recover toties quoties fresh damage is inflicted.

Since the decision of this house in Bonomi v Backhouse it is clear that no action would lie for the excavation. It is not, therefore, a cause of action; that case established that it is the damage and not the excavation which is the cause of action. I cannot understand why every new subsidence, although proceeding from the same original act or omission of the defendants, is not a new cause of action for which damages may be recovered. I cannot concur in the view that there is a breach of duty in the original excavation.”

[64] Diageo also founded upon the following passage of Lord Bramwell at p. 146:

“It seems to me not to matter that the subsidence was of the same spot, nor that the immediate cause of the second subsidence was the non‑existence of coal underneath that spot. Two damages have been occasioned to the plaintiff, one directly and immediately by the removal of the coal under his surface; the other by that and removal of other coal, and consequent creeping and further subsidence. The Attorney General, as I have said, denied that there could be two causes of action if two different parts of the plaintiff’s land subsided at two different times. But surely there must be. Suppose the two pieces belonged to different owners, as I have suggested.

Of course one can see the danger and inconvenience that will follow. This damage accrues many years after the defendant’s act or omission which has caused it. If my reasoning is right, many years hence there might be a further action from some further subsidence. But the inconvenience is as great the other way. For if the defendants are right, it follows that on the least subsidence happening, a cause of action accrues once and for all, the statute of limitations begins to run, and the person injured must bring his action, and claim and recover all damage, actual, possible or contingent for all time.”

[65] The Authority’s position was very much to seek to restrict the Darley Main approach to its facts, in particular founding upon the speech of Lord Bramwell quoted above, and the speech of Lord Fitzgerald. The factual background in Darley Main indicated that while the separate episodes of subsidence occurred several years apart, at the same place, the causative mechanism of the subsidence was somewhat different. This, said the Authority, distinguished the case from the present where it was accepted that the mechanism of the damage was the same for both subsidences.

[66] We think the Authority are taking a somewhat narrow approach to the speeches of Lords Bramwell and Fitzgerald, as it is possible to read them more widely. Lord Bramwell proceeds on the basis that precedent decided that excavation of the coal was not wrongful, and the cause of action accrued when the damage arose (p147). Lord Fitzgerald considered that the disturbance constituted the right of action (p151) and that “A fresh subsidence took place, causing a new and further disturbance of the plaintiff’s enjoyment, which gave him a new and distinct cause of action.” Applying a similar approach here, there had been some years of monitoring, without further settlement, until 2017. So it can be said the 2017 settlement constituted “fresh subsidence” causing further damage.

[67] But in any event Darley Main has been followed in the broad result, and the view of Lord Halsbury has been endorsed by the House of Lords in West Leigh Colliery Company. Lord Macnaghten at p. 29 in a paragraph commencing “It is undoubted law” proceeds to refer to the above passage of Lord Halsbury observing that the surface owner may recover for that damage “as and when it occurs”. Lord Macnaghten further said:

“The damage, not the withdrawal of support, is the cause of action. And so the Statute of Limitations is no bar, however long it may be since the removal was completed; nor is it any answer to the surface owner’s claim to say that he has already brought one or more actions and obtained compensation once again for other damage resulting from the same excavation.”

[68] The Authority sought to distance the present case from this passage because West Leigh was about the validity of a claim for depreciation in the market. However it seems to us that the failure of the claim was very much tied up with the law that the surface owner could claim damages for further subsidence should it occur later. Lord Ashbourne at p. 31 endorses Darley Main Colliery Company and said:

“The mine owner can excavate all he thinks worth taking, subject to the risk of an action on the part of those whose enjoyment of their property he may interfere with, and those who are so interfered with may bring actions as often as a fresh subsidence takes place and their enjoyment of their property is so interfered with.”

[69] Lord James of Hereford at p. 33 comes to the same conclusion and refers to the binding authorities which must prevail.

[70] We also accept that Darley Main has been endorsed in Scotland in Duke of Abercorn in which Lord Mclaren observes that “the adverse view would really mean that the excavation is the cause of action, which would be contrary to the law laid down in Backhouse v Bonomi and Darley Main Colliery Company. ” In other words, it is the damage which is the cause of action. Once this is accepted, it is difficult to disagree with Professor Gordon’s analysis of the authorities at 5-13 leading to “the rule that each fresh subsidence provides a fresh ground of action”.

[71] In these circumstances we do not think we can imply into the 1991 Act a requirement that the validity of a claim for subsequent subsidence damage depends upon the causal mechanism of the subsidence being different in each occasion. This is not how Darley Main has been interpreted and we think would give rise to difficulty in practical application.

[72] We recognise that the 1991 Act makes provision for depreciation payments in sections 10 and 11, which would not appear to have been available at common law. Nevertheless we do not think this is a reason for interpreting the statute inconsistent with the common law, which point was not argued. It is of course possible that a depreciation payment may result, in practical terms, in a “once and for all settlement” with the Authority, if as was indicated, there would be a required discharge of all future claims. We pass no comment upon whether such a settlement would bind future landowners, which point was not debated.

[73] So to conclude we would interpret the 1991 Act in the light of the common law specific to coal mining loss of support cases. On that basis we consider that there is a right to seek remedial action from the Authority for fresh subsidence damage in any case, even if an earlier right to remedy earlier damage is time barred. It follows, therefore, that we do not regard a claim for remediation in respect of the 2017 damage to Warehouse No. 1 to be time‑barred since, on the facts, we regard the 2017 damage to be the result of fresh subsidence.

Conclusion

[74] We consider that a claim for remedial action in respect of damage occurring prior to 2009 to be time‑barred, and we uphold the Authority’s submission in this respect. However we disagree that the single action rule applies under the 1991 Act in cases of fresh subsidence damage. Accordingly we uphold Diageo’s submission in this respect and find that the claim for damage to Warehouse No. 1 in 2017 is not time‑barred. We shall accordingly allow the claim to proceed as accords in respect of the 2017 damage, and also in respect of the sinkhole.

[75] We emphasise that our decision proceeds on an agreed hypothesis of the fact for the purposes of the preliminary hearing. Nothing said here is intended to have a bearing on the merits of the application or parties’ competing views as to actual mechanism of the damage occurring.

[76] Although this opinion deals with a preliminary matter, for avoidance of doubt this opinion is intended to be a decision within the meaning of section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 and the Tribunal Rules.
